11083-the-parables-of-the-saviour-the-go:
The tenth book of the Good Child's Library presents the parables of Jesus in easy verse, with brilliant illuminations from original designs, published in 1851. The publishers aimed to encourage scripture reading by giving children the most interesting New Testament stories in attractive verse, with pictures printed in oil colours, a costly process they pioneered in America.

Fourteen parables follow, from the Sower and the Tares and the Wheat to the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Ten Virgins, and the Judgment. The Barren Fig Tree verses warn that grace refused will not last forever, while the Unjust Judge urges prayer without fainting. The book suits family reading and Sunday schools, teaching Bible stories through rhyme and colour.
11174-four-great-americans-washington-fr:
James Baldwin wrote this schoolroom biography for young Americans, telling four lives in short, plain chapters. Washington the surveyor and general, Franklin the printer and inventor, Webster the orator, and Lincoln the backwoods lawyer turned president. Each life is broken into episodes a child could follow, from Washington's boyhood to Franklin's kite experiment and Lincoln's years in Illinois.

The book's aim is character teaching as much as history, presenting hard work, honesty, and persistence as the thread joining its subjects. Anecdotes carry most of the argument, with battles and politics kept in the background. It still works as an introduction to four figures American schools long treated as models.
11251-famous-reviews-selected-and-edited:
This large anthology collects famous critical reviews with introductory notes, sampling how leading writers judged new books across the nineteenth century and beyond. Reviewers praise, scold, and anatomize novels, poems, and histories, and the editor's notes place each review in its quarrel or moment. The result is less a history of literature than a history of literary opinion.

For students, the volume's value is comparative: the same kinds of praise and blame recur, aimed at very different books. It shows criticism as a public act, shaping reputations in real time. Readers who enjoy literary argument will find the collection's combativeness its main pleasure.
12336-brown-wolf-and-other-jack-london-s:
Franklin K. Mathiews, chief Scout librarian of the Boy Scouts of America, chose this Jack London story collection for young readers. The table of contents runs from Brown Wolf and That Spot through Trust, All Gold Canyon, The Story of Keesh, and The Heathen.

Brown Wolf opens with a woman delaying for dew-wet grass to put on overshoes, then finding a stray dog at her door. Other stories follow gold hunters, Eskimo boys, and sailors, with London usual themes of loyalty, endurance, and the wild. A mid-book tale has Koogah reprove a boaster for notching his stick too coarsely. Mathiews selection softens London harshest work for scouts, but keeps his vigor. The book introduced generations of boys to London.
14630-ruth-fielding-on-cliff-island-or-t:
Alice B. Emerson's Ruth Fielding on Cliff Island, subtitled The Old Hunter's Treasure Box, sends Ruth and her school friends to an island adventure. Cupples and Leon published the illustrated volume in 1915.

Ann flings a rope across a pond to Heavy, the plump girl, while a young fellow wraps the slack round a sapling and urges easy pulling, lest they drag the boat. Treasure hunting, boating, and camp fun follow. The book is a lively girls' series tale, in the Ruth Fielding line, with pluck, friendship, and a mystery at its center.
17498-when-knighthood-was-in-flower-or-t:
Charles Major's Tudor romance, presented as the memoir of Sir Edwin Caskoden, tells the love story of Charles Brandon and the Princess Mary. Chapters run from the Caskodens and a duel to Brandon's coming to court. A lesson in dancing follows, then an honour that makes an enemy, a rare ride to Windsor, and love's fierce sweetness. Trouble in Billingsgate Ward and a warning not to put trust in princesses darken the later pages.

Set in the court of Henry the eighth, the novel mixes history with romance, giving Brandon's rise and his daring love a swashbuckling frame. Readers get one of the most popular American historical romances of its era, full of court intrigue, swordplay, and royal favour. Its charm lies in its brisk pace and its fondness for Tudor colour.
18482-the-most-ancient-lives-of-saint-pa:
Rev. James O'Leary edited this volume of the most ancient lives of Saint Patrick, including the life by Jocelin, hitherto unpublished in America, with Patrick's extant writings. The fifth edition appeared in New York from P. J. Kenedy in 1880, entered for copyright in 1874. A frontispiece shows Saints Columba, Patrick, and Brigida from an engraving made at Paris in 1629.

The lives open with Calphurnius, son of Potitus, a Briton presbyter living near the Irish Sea, who married Conchessa, niece of Martin of Tours. From that family Patrick's story grows, through captivity, calling, and mission to Ireland. A preface and chronological table guide readers through old texts. Readers get Patrick as his earliest biographers told him: apostle, wonder worker, and founder, in lives written centuries after his death.
19144-report-by-the-governor-on-a-visit-:
This 1908 colonial report by the Governor of Newfoundland covers a visit to the Micmac Indians at Bay d'Espoir. Presented to Parliament, it prints the governor's letter, photographs by James Howley, and extracts from official records. The report costs two pence and bears the number fifty-four.

Micmacs, a branch of Algonquins from Maine, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia, reached Newfoundland about a century before, after Beothuks, who had held the land without firearms, were nearly destroyed. A proclamation of 1810 threatened death for murdering a Beothuk. Readers get a short, official ethnographic record of its era.
19155-the-seminole-indians-of-florida-fi:
Clay MacCauley wrote this Smithsonian report on the Seminole Indians of Florida, printed as part of the Bureau of Ethnology's fifth annual report. It describes a small, hard-pressed people after wars with the United States, counting only just over two hundred souls in Florida at the time. Tables break the count by age.

Chapters cover dress, hair, beads, silver disks, homes, food, and social custom, with care for both men and women. MacCauley notes health, climate, and habits as causes of growth or loss. Readers get a detailed ethnographic record, valuable yet framed by the views of its era.
21279-2-b-r-0-2-b:
Kurt Vonnegut Jr. published this short story in Worlds of If in January 1962, taking its title from Hamlet's question, spelled out in digits and letters. Everything is perfectly swell in its future: no prisons, slums, poverty, or wars. All diseases are conquered, and so is old age.

Death, barring accidents, is an adventure for volunteers, and America's population is held at forty million. In a Chicago lying-in hospital, Edward K. Wehling Jr., fifty-six and young by the age's standards, waits for his wife to bear triplets. In this world, new life requires room. The title gives the way out, and the story turns on who must take it.
22037-the-life-public-services-and-selec:
Rutherford B. Hayes rose from Civil War general to Governor of Ohio and then President. Campaign lives like this one introduced such a candidate to the voters. The book traces the Hayes line back to George Hayes of Scotland, who settled at Windsor, Connecticut, in 1682. From that stock, it argues, came a fitting Republican candidate for President.

Family history gives way to war service, Congress, and the governorship. A generous share of the volume prints Hayes's own speeches, so readers could judge his words directly. Such books were tools of persuasion as much as records. This one preserves the image of Hayes that his party carried into the disputed election of 1876.
24639-the-colonial-mortuary-bard-reo-the:
Louis Becke published these three South Seas pieces with T. Fisher Unwin in 1901. The first takes its title from a writer in the Sydney Evening News, who printed amusing entries from a visitors' book at Longwood on St. Helena, where Napoleon died. Becke compares them with mortuary verse from a Melbourne newspaper.

One Melbourne epitaph tells how angels envied fair Emily and whispered they would take her away on Tuesday night. Becke once thought it the noblest mortuary verse ever written, then changed his mind. The companion pieces follow Reo the fisherman and the black bream of Australia, giving readers Becke's wry, salty view of colonial life.
25511-ballads-of-mystery-and-miracle-and:
Frank Sidgwick selects and edits this second series of Popular Ballads of the Olden Time, published in London in 1904. Mystery and miracle supply the first half, with Thomas Rymer, Allison Gross, Tam Lin, the Wife of Usher's Well, and the Great Silkie of Sule Skerrie among the tales.

Fyttes of mirth follow, adding comic and lighter ballads to balance ghosts, fairies, and doomed lovers. The Three Ravens, the Twa Corbies, Young Benjie, and the Lyke-Wake Dirge appear among the later entries. Sidgwick prints the old texts with notes, aiming at a serviceable popular edition that general readers could trust and enjoy.
26021-sioux-indian-courts-an-address-del:
Doane Robinson of Pierre, South Dakota, tells the South Dakota Bar Association about Sioux Indian courts in an address of January 21, 1909. Robinson says the Sioux in their primitive life held an intelligent system of jurisprudence, varying by band as state court practice varies, yet resting on the same broad principles through the confederacy. His authorities were intelligent Sioux men, Hump, One Bull, Wakutemani, and Simon Kirk.

Robinson admits the difficulty of fixing the laws of an unlettered people who now live under conquerors' rules and must trust tradition for old ways. One tale shows a judiciary not wholly incorruptible: guests invited to a feast in a lodge ate their fill, smoked, and forgave a contempt of court. Modern Sioux courts, first proposed by General Harney in 1856 under federal law, get fuller treatment.
26572-chips-from-a-german-workshop-volum:
F. Max Müller published this third volume of Chips from a German Workshop at New York in 1871, gathering essays on literature, biography, and antiquities. Müller, a foreign member of the French Institute, writes as a bridge between German and English letters. He dedicates the book to Francis Turner Palgrave, who helped his first attempts at writing in English.

Essays cover German literature and old German love-songs, a life of Schiller, and Wilhelm Müller, the poet who died in 1827. Joinville, Shakespeare, Bacon in Germany, and a German traveller in England widen the view, while Cornish antiquities and letters from Bunsen, 1848 to 1859, close the volume. It suits readers curious about how German scholarship read the past.
27547-british-borneo-sketches-of-brunai-:
W. H. Treacher, secretary to the Government of Perak and first Governor of British North Borneo, wrote these sketches of Brunai, Sarawak, Labuan, and North Borneo. They were reprinted from the Journal of the Straits Settlements Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society, and printed at Singapore in 1891.

The first chapter runs from the Hudson's Bay Company's charter of 1670 to the British North Borneo Company's charter of November 1881. Treacher notes Friar Odoric in 1322, Portuguese and Spanish visits in 1518 and 1521, and Pigafetta's report of a Chinese trading community. Spanish attacks, Dutch and British connections, diamonds, and an East India Company factory follow. The sketches give a compact colonial history.
2939-william-harvey-and-the-discovery-of:
Thomas Henry Huxley lectured on William Harvey, the Englishman who discovered the circulation of the blood. Harvey was born in 1578 to a small Kent landowner, studied at Cambridge, and lived nearly to eighty, dying in 1657. His father sent the eldest son to university while the other sons went into trade and grew rich.

Huxley contrasts Harvey's account with Galen's older view, under which artery walls actively contracted and dilated like the heart, and the pulse resembled something other than a bag filled and emptied. Harvey showed the blood moves in a circuit, driven by the heart. The lecture honors a discoverer whose experiment overturned fifteen centuries of medical doctrine.
30980-kidnapped-at-the-altar-or-the-roma:
Laura Jean Libbey wrote this melodrama, billed as her new ten-thousand-dollar story, published by the Arthur Westbrook Company in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1909. Its heroine is Jessie Bain, saucy and much loved. Its chapters carry her from young girls finding love so sweet through fate against some people and the girl who plays at flirtation to the mysterious house on Wau-Winet Island.

Later chapters bring a mother's desperate scheme, Gerelda's escape from Wau-Winet Island, a collision with the pilot at the wheel, and love as a poisoned arrow in some hearts. They end with Jessie Bain entering the house of secrets. The closing chapters promise Hubert Varrick rescuing Jessie Bain, after chapters titled I Love Jessie with Heart and Soul and Hubert Cares for Me No Longer. It is a breathless romance of love, peril, and rescue.
31338-an-account-of-the-diseases-which-w:
Donald Monro's 1764 account, printed in London for Millar, Wilson, Durham, and Payne, records the diseases most frequent in British military hospitals in Germany. It covers January 1761 to the troops' return to England in March 1763. Monro, physician to the king's army and to St. George's Hospital, adds an essay on preserving soldiers' health and conducting military hospitals.

Dedicated to the king, whose inquiries into military hospitals in every quarter and concern for suffering officers and soldiers Monro praises, the book aims to ease miseries. Those miseries necessarily attend military life in service. It remains a foundational text of military medicine, grounded in wartime hospital experience.
32860-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume ten, runs alphabetically from Edwardes to Ehrenbreitstein. It opens with Sir Herbert Benjamin Edwardes, soldier-statesman in India, born at Frodesley in 1819, cadet of the East India Company in 1840, and writer for the Delhi Gazette.

Later entries cover Edwards, Eger, Egeria, Egerton, Egg, Egham, Edwardsville, Eglantine, Edwin king of Northumbria, Eglinton, Egmont, egoism, and eel. The longest article treats Egypt, its priesthood in four orders, its temples, and its dynasties, from Psammetichus, who recovered prosperity after Assyrian invasions, to the sack of Thebes. Each entry gives the concise, scholarly treatment of the eleventh edition.
4-lincoln-s-gettysburg-address-given-nov:
On a Pennsylvania battlefield in November 1863, Abraham Lincoln spoke for barely two minutes. His Gettysburg Address dedicated a cemetery for soldiers killed in the Civil War. The speech opens by recalling a nation conceived in liberty and equality.

Lincoln argues the dead have already consecrated the ground beyond any words. The living must carry on their unfinished work so government of, by, and for the people survives. Brief as it is, the address reframed the war as a test of democracy itself. Schoolchildren still memorize its closing lines, and its words mark the cemetery it dedicated.
6588-types-of-children-s-literature-a-co:
Walter Barnes gathers the world's best writing for children into one volume for use in colleges, normal schools, and library schools. The aim, as the publisher states it, is to put knowledge to work for children's needs, and to guide parents and teachers through a vast, rich field. Specimens of each kind of children's writing appear for study and for reading aloud.

Fairy tales, fables, poems, and stories sit side by side, each chosen to show its type at its best. Barnes adds notes to help older readers judge what suits a child and why. Types of Children's Literature is a useful, old-style course book, and a fine shelf of samples for any lover of children's books.
716-the-cruise-of-the-jasper-b:
Don Marquis wrote this light adventure about Clement Cleggett, a New York newspaper man who buys a schooner, the Jasper B, and sails into romance. A bright blade, a skull, and a set of oblong boxes hint at piracy, lost treasure, and old scores. Lady Agatha, in distress, and the villain Logan Black cross his path.

Cleggett stands by his ship through storms, duels, and night raids, while wit and repartee fly as fast as cutlasses. Marquis mixes farce with swashbuckling, and the newspaper man's dry voice keeps the wild plot fun. The book is pure escapist fare, a comic sea romance for readers who like their adventure with a smile.
britannica-1911-b:
B is the second letter of the alphabet. It matches the second symbol of the Phoenician alphabet. It keeps that place in all European alphabets except those drawn from medieval Greek, like Russian. In Greek the old symbol's sound had shifted from b to v, so Slavonic tongues had to invent a fresh sign for the true b sound.

Early forms of the letter looked like nines, and Greek lands reshaped it oddly: upside down at Thera, open-topped elsewhere, almost a C in some Ionic islands. The entry also fixes the sound itself in speech terms. It is a voiced stop made by closing the lips and sounding the voice. It differs from p by that voice. It differs from m by the closed nose passage. Letter shape and lip sound fill its pages.
doe-osti-17019151-synthesis-and-consolid: Tritium breeder ceramics got synthesized and pressed, and this DOE report covers the materials work. The pages record the recipes and the consolidation. The fusion fuel cycle gets its bricks. The ceramics were made. The bricks were baked. The fuel cycle got bricks.
doe-osti-17030340-fy26-final-report-238p: Measuring plutonium-238 in dirt got its FY26 final, and this report covers TIMS measurement in environmental samples. The pages detail the mass spec work. The forensics teams get their method. The report was final. The method was mass spec. The forensics got methods.
doe-osti-2583501-fire-resistance-develop: Fire resistance for UL 790 got developed, and this CRADA final covers the burning brand test. The pages record the fire trials. The roofing folks get their rating. The test was UL 790. The brand was burning. The folks were roofing. The rating was fire.
doe-osti-2997168-solar-spectrum-conversi: Algae bioreactors got their solar spectrum, and this CRADA final covers the conversion approach. The pages record the outcomes. The biofuel folks get their closeout. The conversion was spectrum. The approach was conversion. The folks were biofuel. The closeout was biofuel.
doe-osti-2997302-exploring-multilayer-ne: Integrated deterrence got its network models, and this DOE final builds the scientific basis. The pages detail the multilayer exploration. The strategists get their closeout. The report was final. The models were multilayer network. The strategists got closeouts. The closeout was strategist.
doe-osti-2997409-modular-autonomous-expe: Modular bio experiments got their autonomous platform, and this DOE report covers the biological applications. The pages detail the system. The biologists get their toolkit. The format was short report. The applications were biological. The biologists got toolkits. The toolkit was biologist.
doe-osti-2997410-modular-autonomous-expe: Modular bio experiments got their full report, and this DOE text covers the autonomous platform. The pages detail the complete findings. The biologists get their reference. The format was full report. The findings were complete. The biologists got references. The reference was biologist.
doe-osti-3005839-total-column-infrared-t: Baltimore trace species got column-measured, and this DOE field report covers infrared findings. The pages detail the campaign results. The atmospheric folks get their data. The species were trace infrared. The data were atmospheric. The campaign was Baltimore. The species were column.
doe-osti-3021706-thermal-compton-scatter: Compton scattering got Monte-Carlo-generated, and this DOE text models electron beams. The pages detail the thermal findings. The physicists get their data. The photons were blackbody. The data were physicist. The generator was event. The beams were electron.
doe-osti-3022050-a-guide-for-public-util: Utility commissions got guide-built, and this DOE text recruits technical talent. The pages detail the building findings. The regulators get their data. The capacity was internal technical. The data were regulator. The reform was grid. The talent was recruiting.
doe-osti-3024211-evaluating-energy-savin: Retrofits got workshop-evaluated, and this DOE text saves energy interactively. The pages detail the measure findings. The building folks get their data. The environment was workshop. The data were building. The interactive were retrofits. The building were measures. The workshop was environment.
doe-osti-3365798-implementation-of-a-hig: At many times the speed of sound, air hugs a vehicle's skin in a thin, hot boundary layer. Jonathan Murray implemented a math method that predicts that layer's behavior for any smooth body shape at high Mach numbers. The tool helps designers of hypersonic craft and missiles work faster.
doe-osti-3484473-radiolytic-gas-generati: Mo-99 got gas-generated, and this DOE text covers radiolytic pressure buildup. The pages detail the generation findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The system was closed. The data were nuclear. The Mo-99 were buildup. The closed were system.
famous-reviews-selected-and-edited-with-:
Johnson's Famous Reviews collects landmark book reviews from the great quarterlies. R. Brimley Johnson selected the pieces and added introductory notes. The London title page is dated 1914. A couplet from Pope on authors and critics fronts the contents.

The first section draws on the Edinburgh Review, founded in 1802. Lord Jeffrey appears on Southey's Thalaba and on Wordsworth's Excursion. Lord Brougham on Byron and Sydney Smith on Hannah More follow. Macaulay writes on Southey's Colloquies, Croker's Boswell, and Madame d'Arblay. Anonymous notices treat Wordsworth and Maturin's Melmoth. The Quarterly Review supplies the next section. Johnson frames reviewing as a literary art with its own masters and feuds.
four-great-americans-washington-franklin:
Baldwin tells four lives for young Americans: Washington, Franklin, Webster, and Lincoln. Each story begins in boyhood: Washington the surveyor, Franklin and his whistle, Webster the youngest son. The chapters stay short and plain, built for school readers.

Judge Ebenezer Webster explains where his money will go. He has land enough already, he tells a neighbor; he will try to educate his boys instead. Of his ten children the favorite was a black-haired little fellow called Daniel. James Baldwin, who also retold fifty famous stories, shaped these biographies as models of self-education and public service.
govdocs-archive_org-jfk-assassination-re:
In 2025 the United States government released a new wave of records on the assassination of President John F. Kennedy, under laws requiring the remaining files to come out. Batch two of that release gathers the documents as they were issued.

The papers run to memos, cables, and reports from the agencies that held Kennedy-era files, many of them previously redacted or withheld. Researchers read such batches slowly, comparing versions against earlier releases to find what changed. The file preserves the batch as a public record, complete as issued, for exactly that work.
govdocs-archive_org-national-socialist-a:
The National Socialist Anthology collects writings on the history and works of Heinrich Himmler and certain members of the SS. Its dedication is to Himmler himself, as Reichsführer-SS, which tells the reader plainly where the volume stands.

The anthology presents Nazi material in the movement's own terms, as a record of what its adherents wrote and honored. One technical caution: this copy's text layer is scrambled by a character-substitution cipher, which limits searching and reading on screen. It is presented as an archive holding, without endorsement, for historians of the period.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DukeStevenB_Duk:
Steven Duke wrote on April 2, 1969 to Richard G. Kleindienst, the Deputy Attorney General of the United States. Duke protested a decision by the Justice Department to retry a man named James Miller on narcotics-conspiracy charges. He called the decision a tragic error.

A private citizen writing to the department's second-ranking official is a direct form of protest. Duke put his objection in writing, at the top of the system, where it entered the official file. The letter preserves one voice against a prosecution that its writer believed should never have been brought twice.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ModernPhotoBook:
The FBI's New York office sent this memorandum to the Director, marked for the Latent Fingerprint Section. Its subject line reads 'L/MURKIN,' the bureau's King assassination case. The memo concerns a letter dated September 26, 1967, written by Eric S. Galt to the Modern Photo Bookstore. Galt was the alias James Earl Ray used before the King shooting.

A letter from a suspect, sent to a bookstore months before the crime, was physical evidence. Fingerprints on it could tie a document to a hand. The memo, kept in New York file 44-1609, shows that work in progress. It also shows the bureau still chasing paper from 1967 while the case was being built.
govdocs-archive_org-perspectives-on-init:
René Guénon published Perspectives on Initiation in 1946, near the end of his life. Guénon founded the Traditionalist school, which held that real spiritual teaching passes through unbroken chains of initiation.

The book explains what initiation is and is not: the rites that confer it, the signs by which it is known, and the slow waking of the soul it begins. Guénon separates true initiation from clubs and ceremonies that merely copy its form. For his school, the volume is a key statement of how a seeker actually enters a tradition.
govdocs-archive_org-russian-racial-scien: Russian Racial Science, Volume 2: the volume - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-stepan-bandera-selec: Stepan Bandera: Selected Works, Volume 1 - the made public government document, subject: government records. Held as an archive item; no stance taken, a single volume, dated entry. From the archive shelves, for readers of the literature and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-the-analects-of-conf:
The Analects gathers the sayings of Confucius and his talks with students, recorded by his followers after his death in 479 BC. Presented here in English, the text comes with a learned word-list keyed to book and verse for close study.

Short exchanges carry the teaching: respect for parents, care in speech, rule by moral example rather than force, and learning as a lifelong duty. Those ideas ordered Chinese family life, education, and government for two thousand years. The Analects remains the base of Confucius's school of thought, and this edition's word-list helps readers follow key terms as they recur across the whole work.
govdocs-archive_org-the-book-of-wisdom-b: The Book of Wisdom opens with Book 1, titled The Way of the Creator. The tract sets divine wisdom against worldly folly, urging the reader toward the first and away from the second. It is a devotional work rather than a study, written to guide belief and conduct. The library holds it as a religious volume from its archive set, complete in this first book of the series.
govdocs-archive_org-the-presocratic-phil: The Presocratic Philosophers gathers the earliest Greek thinkers into one volume. It runs from the forerunners who first tried to explain the world's making through to the Sophists of Athens. Thinkers like Heraclitus and Parmenides left only fragments, quoted by later writers. A collection like this one sets those fragments in order so readers can follow the birth of philosophy itself, from water and fire to atoms and argument.
govdocs-archive_org-the-symbolism-of-fre: Freemasonic Symbolism presents Freemasonry as an initiatory institution whose real teaching stays hidden in plain sight. The exposition explains the fraternity's symbols as carriers of that teaching. Masonic signs, tools, and temple forms have drawn curious readers for three centuries. A guide like this one walks through them as a system rather than a code to crack. It serves readers of fraternal history and of the symbolic reading of ritual.
govdocs-archive_org-time-machines-norber: Norbert Jürgen Ratthofer wrote Time Machines about devices classed as stationary and non-stationary. The topic belongs to fringe science: claims that time itself can be engineered. The library holds the work as an archive item, without backing. It serves readers who collect speculative writing on time travel, where physics terms and secret-project stories tend to mix. The volume presents its claims in full for that audience.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-b:
Part B continues David Hume's History of England in the 1860 Virtue edition, three volumes split into six parts. Hume published the history from 1754 to 1762, working backward from the Stuarts to Caesar. His aim was a full national story told with a steady, skeptical mind.

The chapters in each part march year by year through reigns, wars, and parliaments. Hume treats heroes and villains with the same level gaze, which shocked readers used to party histories. The set holds all seventy-one chapters of the complete work. Part B keeps the narrative rolling in the prose that made Hume the most read historian of his century.
jeremy-and-hamlet-a-chronicle-of-certain:
Hugh Walpole published Jeremy and Hamlet in 1923, a chronicle of a boy, a dog, and a country town. He dedicated it to his father and mother as their devoted friend and son. Jeremy is ten and a half and in the lower fourth at school. A new boy, Baltimore, expects Jeremy to shield him from bullying.

Mr. Thompson said you were to see they didn't hit me, Baltimore complains. Jeremy urges him not to call the master Mr. Thompson, since nobody does. Hamlet the dog shares Jeremy's town and school world. Walpole continues the Jeremy books with warmth and close recall.
lincoln-s-gettysburg-address-given-novem:
Abraham Lincoln delivered this address at Gettysburg on November 19, 1863. The battlefield near Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, had become a cemetery ground. Project Gutenberg first issued the text among its earliest etexts. This retranscription was officially re-released on November 19, 1993.

Lincoln opens four score and seven years before his speech. He says the brave men there consecrated the ground already. The living, he argues, must dedicate themselves to unfinished work. The short speech remains America's most famous act of public mourning. The address runs only a few hundred words in full. Gutenberg timed this re-release for the speech's 130th anniversary.
report-by-the-governor-on-a-visit-to-the:
Colonial Reports number 54 prints the Newfoundland governor's report on his visit to the Micmac Indians at Bay d'Espoir. The paper was presented to both Houses of Parliament by command of His Majesty in September 1908. His Majesty's Stationery Office in London sold it for twopence.

The report takes the form of a dispatch from Government House, St. John's, dated July 8, 1908. The governor tells the Secretary of State that he left St. John's on May 28 to visit the Micmac settlement at Bay d'Espoir. His name is not given in the opening lines shown, which begin the journey's account.
ruth-fielding-on-cliff-island-or-the-old: Alice B. Emerson wrote Ruth Fielding on Cliff Island, or The Old Hunter's Treasure Box, issued by Cupples and Leon. Emerson is named as author of Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill and Ruth Fielding at Silver Ranch. A series list follows the title page, pricing each volume at forty cents, postpaid. The list runs from Ruth Fielding of the Red Mill, or Jasper Parloe's Secret, through At Briarwood Hall, At Snow Camp, and At Lighthouse Point. It ends with At Silver Ranch and On Cliff Island itself.
the-cruise-of-the-jasper-b: Don Marquis dedicates The Cruise of the Jasper B. to all copyreaders on all newspapers of America. Its contents list twenty-seven chapters. Their titles are jaunty: A Schooner, a Skipper, and a Skull; Lady Agatha's Story; First Blood for Cleggett; and more. Chapter I, A Bright Blade Leaps from a Rusty Scabbard, begins on an evening in April of a year given as 191-, with Clement J. Cleggett entering. Only the title page, contents, and the opening line are present here.
the-most-ancient-lives-of-saint-patrick-:
Title page and dedication only are present here for The Most Ancient Lives of Saint Patrick, edited with a preface and chronological table by the Rev. James O'Leary. P. J. Kenedy published the fifth edition at New York in 1880, with copyright entered in 1874. No life of the saint appears in these pages.

The title promises the life by Jocelin, hitherto unpublished in America, together with Patrick's extant writings. A frontispiece shows Saints Columba, Patrick, and Brigid, taken from a 1629 Paris engraving by Messingham. O'Leary dedicates the volume to T. W. Croke, Bishop of Auckland in New Zealand, hoping that Croke might one day be counted a St. Patrick for New Zealand.
the-parables-of-the-saviour-the-good-chi: The Parables of the Saviour, in easy verse, is the tenth book of The Good Child's Library, dated 1851, with illuminations from original designs. Only the preface and the series list are present here, so the verses themselves do not appear. The preface says the library aims to encourage a taste for Scripture reading in children. Its pictures, printed in oil colours at great expense, illustrate each history, and twelve books make up the set.
the-seminole-indians-of-florida-fifth-an: Clay MacCauley wrote The Seminole Indians of Florida for the Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of Ethnology. The report forms part of the Bureau's fifth annual report. Its pages shown here give a letter of transmittal and a detailed contents list. No report text itself follows. Chapter one treats personal characteristics, MacCauley's list says. Physique of the men and women, clothing, and personal adornment are covered. Hairdressing, beads, silver disks, and ear rings each get entries. Psychical characteristics and intellectual ability close the chapter. The next chapter begins beyond the portion shown.
theatrum-chemicum-zetzner-1602-b:
A companion gathering from Zetzner's Strasbourg press in 1602 adds more tracts to the Theatrum Chemicum. Lazarus Zetzner kept collecting the chief writers on alchemy in Latin. Together with the first gathering, it helped form one shared canon for the art.

More treatises on the great work fill these pages, in the same grand format. Readers meet famed adepts, their symbols, their furnaces, and their claims. The set gave scattered texts a stable home in print. Anyone who owned both printings held the core library of early modern alchemy, the books that serious students reached for first.
types-of-children-s-literature-a-collect:
Walter Barnes collected and edited Types of Children's Literature for use in colleges, normal schools, and library schools. A publisher's statement frames the aim: direction for parents and teachers choosing from the world's best literature for children. The domain, it says, is vast, rich, and varied.

Barnes's preface explains that the anthology grew from his own classes in children's literature. Students need specimens at hand if they are to know authors, periods, and types by study rather than hearsay. One volume of prose and poetry samples serves both class analysis and children's reading. The book treats children's literature as a field with types worth teaching, not a shelf of accidents.
un-ga-res-49-236-b:
Native peoples won a named place in Guatemala's peace under a deal marked in Resolution 49/236 B. On 31 March 1995, the state and the rebel URNG signed the Agreement on Identity and Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The vote recalls the chain of texts that set up the UN rights mission in Guatemala in 1994, and stretched its term by six months that March.

The mission chief's second report lies before the Assembly. Its counsel, sent to both the state and the URNG, weighs how each kept its pledges under the rights deal. The text takes note of that counsel in full. The native deal, with the rights mission to check it, formed one pillar of the peace that ended the war in 1996.
un-ga-res-51-198-b:
Guatemala's peace deals needed a UN watch, and Resolution 51/198 B keeps that watch in place. The Mission for the Verification of Human Rights in Guatemala had been set up in 1994. In December 1996, the government and the rebel URNG signed a firm and lasting peace at Guatemala City. The vote stretches the mission's mandate for one year, to 31 March 1998, in a fresh form fit for peace.

The text recalls the chain of votes that built the mission, from 1990 on. The Secretary-General was asked to counsel how the mission's shape and staff should change for its new task. That task: check that the pledges of the peace, on rights and far more, were kept in daily life.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 49/236 B, adopted on 14 September 1995, renewed the Guatemala human rights verification mission for six months, until 18 March 1996. The Assembly stressed the weight of the Agreement on Identity and Rights of Indigenous Peoples, signed by the parties on 31 March 1995. It called it a landmark in the International Decade of the World's Indigenous People.

The parties were told to carry out the mission director's advice from his first and second reports. They were told to keep their human rights promises, now including the indigenous peoples agreement's rights parts. The text also urges agreement on land and economic questions, the next item in the talks, toward an early final peace.

General Assembly Resolution 51/198 B, adopted on 27 March 1997, reshaped the United Nations presence in Guatemala after peace. The final peace accord of 29 December 1996 had ended the long internal conflict. Work was under way on checking the ceasefire, pulling forces apart, and disarming and demobilizing fighters. Military observers attached to the mission watched that work.

The Assembly renamed the human rights mission the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala. It renewed it for one year, until 31 March 1998, to verify all the peace accords. Both parties were praised for their steady search for peace and called on to keep every promise they had made.
when-knighthood-was-in-flower-or-the-lov: Only the title pages are present here for When Knighthood Was in Flower, so the tale itself does not appear. Edwin Caskoden, the pen name of Charles Major, rewrote the love story of Charles Brandon and Mary Tudor in modern English. Mary was the sister of King Henry the Eighth. The book claims to rest on a memoir by Sir Edwin Caskoden. This Julia Marlowe edition adds scenes from the play. Bowen-Merrill of Indianapolis printed it, with copyright dates of 1898 and 1901.
william-harvey-and-the-discovery-of-the-:
Thomas H. Huxley gave a lecture on William Harvey and the discovery of the circulation of the blood. Harvey, born in 1578, lived to 1657, nearly eighty years old. He was the eldest son of a small Kent landowner who sent him to Cambridge. His brothers went into trade and grew rich.

Harvey then studied at Padua in Italy, under the famed Fabricius of Aquapendente. Back in London he joined the College of Physicians and rose fast in practice. By about 1616 the college made him its professor of anatomy. Huxley traces how Harvey's work in that post led to his great find on the blood's circuit. Science and one man's patience fill the talk.
